title: Sum an Array
statement:
Add up every element of an array of 32-bit integers.

## Your procedure

```
int sum_array(const int *values, int count);
```

Return the total. An empty array sums to `0`.

## The calling convention

Microsoft x64. The first four integer or pointer arguments arrive in
registers, and a 32-bit result goes back in `eax`:

| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | return |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 64-bit | `rcx` | `rdx` | `r8` | `r9` | `rax` |
| 32-bit | `ecx` | `edx` | `r8d` | `r9d` | `eax` |

`rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`-`r11` are yours to clobber. `rbx`, `rbp`, `rsi`,
`rdi` and `r12`-`r15` belong to the caller: use one and you must `push` it on
the way in and `pop` it on the way out.

Nothing here needs the stack, so nothing here needs a prologue.

## Watch out

- `count` may be `0`, and `values` may then be a null pointer -- so test the
  count *before* the first load, not after.
- The elements are 4 bytes wide. `[rcx + r8*4]` walks them with the scale
  factor doing the arithmetic for you; `dword ptr` says how much to read.
- The totals here fit comfortably in 32 bits, so `eax` is wide enough.
starter_code:
; int sum_array(const int *values, int count)
;
;   rcx = values (the array)
;   edx = count  (how many elements)
;   eax = the total you return

.code
sum_array PROC
    ; your code here
    xor eax, eax
    ret
sum_array ENDP
end

tests.name: empty array
tests.description: count is 0 and values is NULL -- the count must be tested before anything is loaded.

tests.name: negatives cancel out
tests.description: A total of zero is a real answer, not an empty array.
